let you cease your glory. You must not burn for war against these Trojans. Mad men lusting for battle. Now about me. You will only make my glory that much less. Me, all cares about is me. Petulis, he can go to battle, but don't win too much glory. Do not outshine me.

So, because he says this, what does Petus do? He tries to win all the glory for himself. He engages in a duel with Hector and it costs him his life. So, it's Achilles fault this is happening and he knows it. The psychology here is just so insightful, so deep, so striking.

Okay, let's pretend John and Jill are boyfriend girlfriend, but they have a fight like boyfriend and girlfriend do and they break up. But they want to long for each other, but don't want to apologize to each other. So, Jill tells her best friend Jane to talk to John to try to get him to apologize.

And then Jane goes talks to John and John says, "You know what? I've had it with Jill. I'd much rather date you because you're more beautiful and you're more reasonable." And then Jason is really excited because Jill is prettier than she is, right? So she runs back to Jill and says,

"Hey, John asked me to go on a date. Maybe I can use this opportunity to convince him to apologize." And then Jill says, "Okay, go date him, but what if you do? Don't kiss him."

So what does Jill do? Right? This is reverse psychology. So Jill knows that if she says this, Jane's going to kiss John. And Achilles knows that if he tells Petus, "Don't win too much glory," but is going to win a lot of glory, right?

And so what happens of course is that Procles dies now Achilles can now enter the battlefield and win all the glory for himself. And that's what happens. He kills Hector. He saves the Greeks.

But then he goes crazy. What he does is he ties Hector to his chariot and he starts riding around the walls of Troy. It's a war crime. It's disgusting. It's hideous. The children are going crazy. But the Greeks are like, "We don't want this, man." The gods are like, "What the hell's going on?" So now we move to the end of the Iliad and at this point Priam cannot sleep because his son Hector is being mutilated by Achilles.

Achilles can't sleep because he cannot forgive himself for the death of Procles. And so he takes it out on Hector. The gods are watching this and they're kind of disgusted. The games are over now, the gathered army scattered. Each man to his fashion; fighters turned their minds from thoughts of food and the sweet warm grip of sleep. But Achilles kept on grieving for his friend, the memory burning on and all subduing sleep could not take him.

But not now he turned and twisted side to side. He lost manhood, his gallant heart. What rough campaigns they fought to an end together. What hardships they had suffered, cleaving their way through wars of men and pounding waves at sea. The memories flooded over him, live tears flowing.

And now he lay on his side, then flat on his back, then face down again. At least at last he leapt to his feet, one in anguish and amish along the surf and dawn on dawn. He cannot sleep. He's depressed. He is racked with self-guilt. He cannot forgive himself for what has happened.

Flaming over the sea and shore would find him pacing. Then he yokes his racing team to the chariot harness, lashing the corpse of Hector behind the car for dragging and hauls him three times round the dead Procles' tomb. And then he rests again in his tents and leaves the body sprawled face down in the dust.

But pity Hector dead men though he was and wards all corruption off from Hector's corpse and around him head to foot. The great god wrapped the golden shield of storm so his skin would never rip as Achilles dragged him on.

And so he kept on raging, shaming noble Hector. But the gods in bliss looked down and pitied Priam's son. They kept urging the sharp-eyed giant killer Hermes to go and steal the body. A plan that pleased them all.
